claim: Recurrent loss of pelvic appendages in sticklebacks has been linked to natural mutations in a pelvic enhancer that maps upstream of Pitx1.
source: Recurrent loss of pelvic appendages in sticklebacks has previously been linked to natural mutations in a pelvic enhancer that maps upstream of Pitx1.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work, as indicated by the word 'previously'.

claim: The sequence of the upstream PelA enhancer is not conserved to mammals.
source: The sequence of this upstream PelA enhancer is not conserved to mammals
evidence: This is a factual statement about sequence conservation that can be verified through comparative genomic analysis.

claim: A new pelvic enhancer, PelB, maps downstream rather than upstream of Pitx1.
source: Here we identify a new pelvic enhancer, PelB, that maps downstream rather than upstream of Pitx1.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: PelB drives expression in the posterior portion of the developing hind limb.
source: PelB drives expression in the posterior portion of the developing hind limb
evidence: This is supported by transgenic reporter assays shown in the figures.

claim: Deleting the PelB sequence from mice alters the size of several hind limb structures.
source: deleting the sequence from mice alters the size of several hind limb structures.
evidence: This is supported by morphological measurements presented in the study.

claim: PelB sequences are broadly conserved from fish to mammals.
source: PelB sequences are broadly conserved from fish to mammals.
evidence: This is supported by comparative sequence analysis shown in the figures.

claim: A wild stickleback population lacking the pelvis has an insertion/deletion mutation that disrupts the structure and function of PelB.
source: A wild stickleback population lacking the pelvis has an insertion/deletion mutation that disrupts the structure and function of PelB
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data and functional assays in sticklebacks.

claim: Changes in the PelB enhancer contribute to evolutionary modification of pelvic appendages in nature.
source: changes in this ancient enhancer contribute to evolutionary modification of pelvic appendages in nature.
evidence: This is inferred from the functional data showing reduced enhancer activity in pelvic-reduced populations.

claim: Bats, birds, and flying fish have greatly elongated pectoral appendages compared to pelvic appendages.
source: For example, bats, birds, and flying fish have greatly elongated pectoral appendages compared to pelvic appendages.
evidence: This is established knowledge about vertebrate morphology.

claim: Whales, manatees, and several fish groups have reduced or lost their pelvic appendages, while retaining robust pectoral appendages.
source: Conversely, whales, manatees, and several fish groups have reduced or lost their pelvic appendages, while retaining robust pectoral appendages.
evidence: This is established knowledge about vertebrate morphology.

claim: Tbx5 is expressed in the developing forelimb.
source: Tbx5 is expressed in the developing forelimb (Gibson-Brown et al., 1996)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Complete loss of Tbx5 prevents proper forelimb outgrowth.
source: complete loss of this gene prevents proper forelimb outgrowth (Ahn et al., 2002; Garrity et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Tbx4 is expressed specifically in the developing hind limb.
source: Tbx4 is expressed specifically in the developing hind limb (Chapman et al., 1996)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Loss of one or both copies of Tbx4 results in significant hind limb defects.
source: loss of one or both copies results in significant hind limb defects (Naiche and Papaioannou, 2003; Bongers et al., 2004; Naiche and Papaioannou, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Pitx1 encodes a homeodomain transcription factor that acts upstream of Tbx4.
source: Pitx1, which encodes a homeodomain transcription factor that acts upstream of Tbx4 (Logan and Tabin, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The hind limb-specific expression pattern of Pitx1 is conserved in many different vertebrates, including fish, birds, and mammals.
source: The hind limb-specific expression pattern of Pitx1 is conserved in many different vertebrates, including fish, birds, and mammals (Lanctôt et al., 1997; Logan et al., 1998; Shapiro et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Pitx1 knockout mice show reduced hind limb size, complete loss of the ilium and patella, and altered shape of the remaining hind limb bones.
source: Pitx1 knockout mice show reduced hind limb size, complete loss of the ilium and patella, and altered shape of the remaining hind limb bones (Lanctôt et al., 1999; Szeto et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Mutations in the Pitx1 gene or its surrounding regulatory regions are associated with avian foot feathering.
source: Mutations in the Pitx1 gene or its surrounding regulatory regions are also associated with avian foot feathering (Domyan et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Mutations in the Pitx1 gene or its surrounding regulatory regions are associated with human polydactyly.
source: several human limb abnormalities, including polydactyly (Klopocki et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Mutations in the Pitx1 gene or its surrounding regulatory regions are associated with Liebenberg syndrome.
source: Liebenberg syndrome (Spielmann et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Mutations in the Pitx1 gene or its surrounding regulatory regions are associated with familial clubfoot.
source: familial clubfoot (Gurnett et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Mice with a complete knockout of Pitx1 die soon after birth with pituitary gland abnormalities, shortened jaws, and cleft palate.
source: Mice with a complete knockout of Pitx1 die soon after birth with pituitary gland abnormalities, shortened jaws, and cleft palate (Lanctôt et al., 1999; Szeto et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Pitx1 is a major effect locus controlling pelvic reduction that has evolved repeatedly in many freshwater stickleback populations.
source: Genetic crosses between wild stickleback fish have shown that Pitx1 is a major effect locus controlling pelvic reduction that has evolved repeatedly in many freshwater populations (Cresko et al., 2004; Shapiro et al., 2004; Coyle et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The Pel enhancer (PelA) drives expression specifically in the developing pelvic hind fin.
source: High-resolution genetic mapping and enhancer studies identified a non-coding regulatory sequence located upstream of Pitx1, called Pel, that drives expression specifically in the developing pelvic hind fin (Chan et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The Pel enhancer has been independently deleted in many pelvic-reduced freshwater populations.
source: The Pel enhancer has been independently deleted in many pelvic-reduced freshwater populations, accompanied by molecular signatures of positive selection centered around the Pel deletions (Chan et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Reintroduction of Pel-driven Pitx1 can restore pelvic development in pelvic-reduced sticklebacks.
source: Reintroduction of Pel-driven Pitx1 can restore pelvic development in pelvic-reduced sticklebacks, providing strong evidence that regulatory changes in Pitx1 underlie the repeated loss of pelvic hind fins in wild sticklebacks (Chan et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Pel enhancer orthologs can be identified in other fish, but not in most other vertebrates, including mammals.
source: Pel enhancer orthologs can be identified in other fish, but not in most other vertebrates, including mammals (Chan et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The BAC scan covered an 850 kb region of the Pitx1 locus.
source: To identify regulatory sequences that drive limb expression in developing mouse embryos, we surveyed an 850 kb region of the Pitx1 locus using overlapping mouse BAC clones
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: The BAC scan includes 607 kb of sequence upstream of the Pitx1 coding region.
source: Note that the scan includes 607 kb of sequence upstream of the Pitx1 coding region.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: Two large deletions associated with human forelimb abnormalities map upstream of the Pitx1 gene.
source: Two large deletions associated with human forelimb abnormalities also map upstream of the Pitx1 gene (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 1 and prior knowledge.

claim: Both deletions associated with human forelimb abnormalities remove the flanking H2afy gene and bring a far upstream enhancer called hs1473 closer to the human Pitx1 gene.
source: Both deletions remove the flanking H2afy gene and bring a far upstream enhancer called hs1473 closer to the human Pitx1 gene (Spielmann et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The hs1473 enhancer can drive gene expression in both forelimbs and hind limbs.
source: The hs1473 enhancer can drive gene expression in both forelimbs and hind limbs (Pennacchio et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The hs1473 enhancer has been named the pan-limb enhancer or Pen.
source: has hence been named the pan-limb enhancer or Pen (Kragesteen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Ectopic expression of Pitx1 in forelimbs likely causes the arm-to-leg-like morphological abnormalities characteristic of human Liebenberg syndrome.
source: Ectopic expression of Pitx1 in forelimbs likely causes the arm-to-leg-like morphological abnormalities characteristic of human Liebenberg syndrome (Spielmann et al., 2012; Kragesteen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and uses the word 'likely' indicating inference.

claim: A deletion associated with lowered Pitx1 expression in hind limbs and feathered feet in birds maps upstream of the H2afy gene.
source: A deletion associated with lowered Pitx1 expression in hind limbs and feathered feet in birds also maps upstream of the H2afy gene (Domyan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Two different BAC clones drove lacZ expression in the pituitary gland.
source: In our initial screen, two different BAC clones drove lacZ expression in the pituitary gland, a well-known site of endogenous Pitx1 expression (BACs RP24-296G14 and RP24-353M13, see Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the BAC screen.

claim: The two BAC clones that drove pituitary expression overlap in a 29 kb region.
source: These two BACs overlap in a 29 kb region, suggesting this shared region may contain a pituitary enhancer.
evidence: This is based on data from the BAC screen and inference about enhancer location.

claim: The shared 29 kb region contains a sequence called the Pitx1 Distal Enhancer (PDE).
source: Interestingly, this shared region also contains a sequence called the Pitx1 Distal Enhancer (PDE, Figure 1)
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 1 and prior knowledge.

claim: The PDE region shows significant chromatin interactions in limb tissues with the promoter of Pitx1.
source: a region that shows significant chromatin interactions in limb tissues with the promoter of Pitx1 (Sarro et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The PDE region has been knocked out in mice, leading to modest reductions in Pitx1 expression in limbs and mandibles, but no detectable limb or jaw skeletal phenotypes.
source: This region has been knocked out in mice, leading to modest reductions in Pitx1 expression in limbs and mandibles, but no detectable limb or jaw skeletal phenotypes (Sarro et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: A 2.5 kb subregion of the PDE region can drive consistent expression in the developing pituitary and has been named the Pit enhancer.
source: However, a 2.5 kb subregion of the PDE region can drive consistent expression in the developing pituitary, and this region has now been named the Pit enhancer (Kragesteen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Three different BAC clones drove lacZ expression in the developing forelimb.
source: Three different BAC clones drove lacZ expression in the developing forelimb (Figure 1C,I,O).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the BAC screen shown in Figure 1.

claim: Only one BAC clone (RP23-55J18) drove prominent expression in both forelimb and hind limb.
source: However, only one of these clones, BAC RP23-55J18, also drove prominent expression in the hind limb.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the BAC screen.

claim: BAC RP23-55J18 drove lacZ expression at the proximal end of the forelimb autopod and the posterior side of the hind limb autopod.
source: With this clone, lacZ expression was observed at the proximal end of the forelimb autopod (Figure 1C), as well as the posterior side of the hind limb autopod (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the BAC screen shown in Figure 1.

claim: Multiple limb enhancers may exist in the Pitx1 region.
source: it is possible that multiple limb enhancers exist in the Pitx1 region
evidence: This is speculation based on the expression patterns observed.

claim: Evolutionarily conserved sequences and tissue-specific chromatin marks can be used to identify tissue-specific enhancers.
source: Previous studies suggest that evolutionarily conserved sequences and tissue-specific chromatin marks can often be used to identify tissue-specific enhancers (Fortini and Rubin, 1990; Mortlock et al., 2003; Woolfe et al., 2005; Pennacchio et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: A 9466 bp region downstream of Pitx1 contains multiple conserved sequences with increased DNaseI accessibility during hind limb development.
source: A 9466 bp region downstream of Pitx1, and located within a large intron of the Pcbd2 gene, contains multiple conserved sequences with increased DNaseI accessibility during hind limb development (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The 9466 bp region downstream of Pitx1 directly interacts with the Pitx1 promoter in hind limbs but not forelimbs of developing mouse embryos.
source: Chromosome conformation capture experiments (Andrey et al., 2017) show that this region directly interacts with the Pitx1 promoter in hind limbs but not forelimbs of developing mouse embryos, consistent with the region serving as a possible Pitx1 enhancer (Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The 9466 bp region downstream of Pitx1 is enriched for H3K27ac signal in developing hind limbs versus forelimbs of both mouse and lizard embryos.
source: The same region is enriched for H3K27ac signal in developing hind limbs versus forelimbs of both mouse and lizard embryos (Infante et al., 2015), suggesting the region may contain evolutionarily conserved hind limb enhancer activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work and data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: A lacZ expression construct containing the 9466 bp region drove strong and reproducible lacZ expression in the hind limbs but not forelimbs of transient transgenic E12.5 embryos.
source: A lacZ expression construct containing this region drove strong and reproducible lacZ expression in the hind limbs but not forelimbs of transient transgenic E12.5 embryos (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from transgenic reporter assays shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The full-length PelB fragment showed strongest expression in the posterior half of the developing autopod, with weaker expression at the proximal junction of hind limb and body wall.
source: Strongest expression was observed in the posterior half of the developing autopod, with weaker expression also seen at the proximal junction of hind limb and body wall.
evidence: This is a primary finding from transgenic reporter assays.

claim: A 2173 bp subregion (PelBcon1) exhibited the same proximal expression as the full-length PelB fragment.
source: A 2173 bp subregion (PelBcon1), containing a hind limb-enriched open chromatin domain and sequence conservation through amphibia, exhibited the same proximal expression as the full-length fragment (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from transgenic reporter assays shown in Figure 2C.

claim: A 3280 bp subregion (PelBcon2) exhibited the same autopod pattern as the full-length PelB fragment.
source: A separate, non-overlapping 3280 bp subregion (PelBcon2), with a strong hind limb-enriched DNase peak and sequence conservation through teleosts, exhibited the same autopod pattern as the full-length fragment (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from transgenic reporter assays shown in Figure 2D.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9 targeting was used to delete a 9425 bp region from the endogenous mouse locus, encompassing virtually the entire PelB region.
source: To test whether PelB is required for normal hind limb development, we used CRISPR/Cas9 targeting to delete a 9425 bp region from the endogenous mouse locus, encompassing virtually the entire PelB region tested in the lacZ assay (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: The PelB deletion allele was transmitted through the germline.
source: The deletion allele was transmitted through the germline
evidence: This is a primary finding from the mouse genetics experiments.

claim: PelB heterozygotes and homozygotes were born in expected Mendelian ratios.
source: subsequent crosses showed that PelB heterozygotes and homozygotes were born in expected Mendelian ratios
evidence: This is a primary finding from the mouse genetics experiments.

claim: PelB heterozygotes and homozygotes showed normal viability and fertility.
source: showed normal viability and fertility.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the mouse genetics experiments.

claim: Loss of the PelB enhancer reduced Pitx1 levels to approximately 85% of control levels in E12.5 hind limbs.
source: Quantitative RT-PCR experiments of developing wild type and PelB homozygous mutant embryos showed that loss of the PelB enhancer reduced Pitx1 levels to approximately 85% of control levels in E12.5 hind limbs (p<0.05, Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from qRT-PCR experiments.

claim: Loss of the PelB enhancer did not significantly change Pcbd2 expression.
source: In contrast, no significant change was seen in Pcbd2 expression (Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from qRT-PCR experiments.

claim: PelB acts as an enhancer of the Pitx1 gene during normal development.
source: These results suggest that PelB acts as an enhancer of the Pitx1 gene during normal development
evidence: This is inferred from the qRT-PCR data showing reduced Pitx1 expression.

claim: Additional control regions contribute to overall levels of Pitx1 hind limb expression.
source: but that additional control regions also must contribute to overall levels of Pitx1 hind limb expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the incomplete reduction of Pitx1 expression upon PelB deletion.

claim: One Pitx1PelB-/PelB- mouse exhibited right hind limb preaxial polydactyly.
source: One Pitx1PelB-/PelB- mouse exhibited right hind limb preaxial polydactyly, an alteration known to occur at low background rates in the C57BL/6J mouse background (Dagg, 1966).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the skeletal analysis.

claim: Preaxial polydactyly occurs at low background rates in the C57BL/6J mouse background.
source: an alteration known to occur at low background rates in the C57BL/6J mouse background (Dagg, 1966).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: No major changes in the number, or presence or absence of hind limb, forelimb, or jaw bones were apparent in Pitx1PelB-/PelB- animals compared to wild type.
source: No other major changes in the number, or presence or absence of hind limb, forelimb, or jaw bones were apparent in Pitx1PelB-/PelB- animals as compared to wild type.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the skeletal analysis.

claim: Significant quantitative reductions were seen in the length of several hind limb bones in homozygous PelB mutant mice.
source: However, significant quantitative reductions were seen in the length of several hind limb bones in the homozygous PelB mutant mice, confirming that the PelB enhancer sequence is required for normal developmental size of hind limb structures (Figure 3, Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the skeletal analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The PelB enhancer sequence is required for normal developmental size of hind limb structures.
source: confirming that the PelB enhancer sequence is required for normal developmental size of hind limb structures
evidence: This is inferred from the skeletal measurements showing reduced bone lengths.

claim: Pitx1null/null mice show severe hind limb deformities, facial abnormalities, and neonatal lethality.
source: Pitx1null/null mice show severe hind limb deformities, facial abnormalities, and neonatal lethality (Lanctôt et al., 1999; Szeto et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Heterozygous Pitx1null/+ mice are reported to be phenotypically normal, with a small percentage exhibiting a club foot phenotype.
source: By contrast, heterozygous Pitx1null/+ mice are reported to be phenotypically normal, with a small percentage exhibiting a club foot phenotype (Alvarado et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: All heterozygous carriers of the Pitx1 null mutation were smaller than non-carriers.
source: All heterozygous carriers of the Pitx1 null mutation were smaller than non-carriers, with significant reduction of jaw and several hind limb elements after correcting for body size (Supplementary file 1E).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the skeletal analysis.

claim: Pitx1null/PelB- mice showed significant reductions in length of the jaw and several hind limb bones compared to Pitx1null/+ animals.
source: In addition, Pitx1null/PelB- mice showed significant reductions in length of the jaw and several hind limb bones compared to Pitx1null/+ animals (Supplementary file 1F).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the skeletal analysis.

claim: Pitx1null/PelB- mice showed complete absence of patellae.
source: The most striking phenotype was a complete absence of patellae in Pitx1null/PelB- mice (Figure 4K,L).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the skeletal analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Patellae are completely missing in Pitx1null/null mice.
source: For comparison, patellae are completely missing in Pitx1null/null mice (Lanctôt et al., 1999; Szeto et al., 1999)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Patellae are smaller but consistently present in Pitx1null/+ heterozygous animals.
source: and are smaller but consistently present in the Pitx1null/+ heterozygous animals in our crosses (Figure 4H,I).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the skeletal analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Patellae are found in hind limbs but not forelimbs of many vertebrates.
source: Patellae are found in hind limbs but not forelimbs of many vertebrates (Samuels et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Loss of the patella in the compound crosses suggests that PelB contributes to the development of the patella.
source: loss of the patella in the compound crosses suggests that PelB also contributes to the development of this structure.
evidence: This is inferred from the phenotype observed in Pitx1null/PelB- mice.

claim: The patella is a large sesamoid bone embedded in the tendon connecting the femur and tibia.
source: The patella is a large sesamoid bone embedded in the tendon connecting the femur and tibia (Samuels et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The patella arises from dorsal limb bud mesenchyme cells and requires muscular contraction for normal development.
source: Embryological studies show that the patella arises from dorsal limb bud mesenchyme cells and requires muscular contraction for normal development (Eyal et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: PelB expressing cells in the posterior limb bud may contribute descendants to the dorsal limb bud domain that forms the patella.
source: It is possible that PelB expressing cells in the posterior limb bud contribute descendants to the dorsal limb bud domain that forms the patella, or to domains that form more anterior skeletal structures.
evidence: This is speculation about possible mechanisms.

claim: Descendants of Shh expressing cells in the posterior limb bud expand and contribute to multiple skeletal structures outside the initial expression domain.
source: For comparison, previous fate mapping experiments have shown that the descendants of Shh expressing cells in the posterior limb bud expand and contribute to multiple skeletal structures outside the initial expression domain (Harfe et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Loss of the PelB enhancer could have indirect effects on the patella or more anterior skeletal structures by altering overall chromatin configuration of the Pitx1 locus.
source: Alternatively, loss of the PelB enhancer could have indirect effects on either the patella or more anterior skeletal structures, for example by altering overall chromatin configuration of the Pitx1 locus (Kragesteen et al., 2018)
evidence: This is speculation about possible mechanisms supported by a citation.

claim: Loss of the PelB enhancer could have indirect effects by perturbing cell non-autonomous signaling pathways involved in limb formation.
source: by perturbing cell non-autonomous signaling pathways involved in limb formation
evidence: This is speculation about possible mechanisms.

claim: Loss of the PelB enhancer could have indirect effects by altering patterns of muscular activity that influence formation of some skeletal structures.
source: or by altering patterns of muscular activity that also influence formation of some skeletal structures.
evidence: This is speculation about possible mechanisms.

claim: Many vertebrate genes have multiple 'functionally redundant' enhancers that drive similar patterns in a particular tissue.
source: Recent studies (Osterwalder et al., 2018) have proposed that many vertebrate genes have multiple 'functionally redundant' enhancers that drive similar patterns in a particular tissue, with each enhancer making purely quantitative contributions to the overall level of expression of a gene.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: PelB is active in the hind limbs of mice but not throughout the entire hind limb.
source: First, while PelB is active in the hind limbs of mice, it is clearly not active throughout the entire hind limb
evidence: This is based on the expression pattern data from transgenic assays.

claim: Two different hind limb enhancers have been identified in the Tbx4 gene of mammals (HLEA and HLEB).
source: For example, two different hind limb enhancers have previously been identified in the Tbx4 gene of mammals (HLEA and HLEB).
evidence: This is supported by the context indicating prior work.

claim: The two Tbx4 enhancers drive expression patterns that overlap in some regions of the hind limb, but each enhancer also has unique spatial expression patterns.
source: Although these two enhancers drive expression patterns that overlap in some regions of the hind limb, each enhancer also has unique spatial expression patterns not shared with the other enhancer (Menke et al., 2008; Infante et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Significant phenotypes are seen in laboratory animals engineered to lack individual enhancers.
source: Second, significant phenotypes are seen in laboratory animals engineered to lack individual enhancers, a result that clearly demonstrates the enhancers are not functionally redundant at the organismal level.
evidence: This is based on the data from this study and prior work.

claim: Knockout of HLEA alone produces significant changes in length of hind limb elements.
source: Knockout of HLEA alone produces significant changes in length of hind limb elements, even if additional, or more severe, phenotypes are detected when analyzed on a genetic background heterozygous for a Tbx4 null mutation (Menke et al., 2008; Infante et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Mutations of individual Pitx1 enhancers have made significant contributions to adaptive evolution of skeletal phenotypes in wild populations.
source: Third, mutations of individual Pitx1 enhancers have clearly made significant contributions to adaptive evolution of skeletal phenotypes in wild populations.
evidence: This is based on data from this study and prior work on sticklebacks.

claim: Many pelvic-reduced sticklebacks show complete deletion of the PelA but not the PelB enhancer in natural environments.
source: Many pelvic-reduced sticklebacks show complete deletion of the PelA but not the PelB enhancer in natural environments, as well as molecular signatures of adaptive selection that are centered on the PelA region (Chan et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Loss of the PelA enhancer alone is sufficient to produce evolutionarily significant pelvic reduction in some wild populations.
source: These results suggest that loss of the PelA enhancer alone is sufficient to produce evolutionarily significant pelvic reduction in some wild populations.
evidence: This is inferred from the data on PelA deletions in wild populations.

claim: The PelA enhancer of sticklebacks is alignable in fish but not tetrapods.
source: Because the PelA enhancer of sticklebacks is alignable in fish but not tetrapods
evidence: This is based on sequence conservation analysis.

claim: The Pen enhancer is found in tetrapods but not fish.
source: while the Pen enhancer is found in tetrapods but not fish
evidence: This is based on sequence conservation analysis.

claim: Hind limb specific regulation of Pitx1 may have arisen by different mechanisms in fish and tetrapod lineages.
source: it has recently been proposed that hind limb specific regulation of Pitx1 may have arisen by different mechanisms in fish and tetrapod lineages (Kragesteen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The Pen enhancer drives expression in both forelimbs and hind limbs unless silenced by other elements.
source: Within tetrapods, the Pen enhancer also drives expression in both forelimbs and hind limbs unless silenced by other elements
evidence: This is based on prior knowledge about the Pen enhancer.

claim: The ancestral form of Pitx1 expression may have been pan-limb rather than hind limb-specific.
source: raising the possibility that the ancestral form of Pitx1 expression was actually pan-limb rather than hind limb-specific
evidence: This is speculation based on the properties of the Pen enhancer.

claim: Distinct Pitx1 expression patterns and distinct morphology of forelimbs and hind limbs may have evolved as subsequent events in the tetrapod lineage.
source: and that distinct Pitx1 expression patterns and distinct morphology of forelimbs and hind limbs evolved as subsequent events in the tetrapod lineage (Kragesteen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is speculation supported by a citation.

claim: The PelB enhancer sequence is conserved between fish and mammals.
source: In contrast, our data identify a Pitx1 enhancer whose sequence is clearly conserved between fish and mammals
evidence: This is based on sequence conservation analysis presented in the study.

claim: The PelB enhancer drives expression in pelvic rather than pectoral appendages when functionally tested in both sticklebacks and mice.
source: and that also drives expression in pelvic rather than pectoral appendages when functionally tested in both sticklebacks and mice.
evidence: This is based on transgenic reporter assays presented in the study.

claim: Pelvic-appendage-specific enhancers of the Pitx1 gene are a shared and ancient genomic feature that existed in the common ancestor of both fish and land animals.
source: These data show that pelvic-appendage-specific enhancers of the Pitx1 gene are a shared and ancient genomic feature that already existed in the common ancestor of both fish and land animals.
evidence: This is inferred from the conservation and functional data on PelB.

claim: An ancient and ancestral PelB-based regulatory mechanism may have been modified by evolution of separate lineage-specific PelA and Pen-based regulatory sequences in teleost fish and tetrapods.
source: An ancient and ancestral PelB-based regulatory mechanism may have subsequently been modified by evolution of separate lineage-specific PelA and Pen-based regulatory sequences in teleost fish and tetrapods.
evidence: This is speculation about evolutionary mechanisms.

claim: PelA-like and Pen-like functions may be ancient like PelB, even though the primary sequence of these enhancers are no longer alignable because of turnover of binding sites at the DNA sequence level.
source: Alternatively, PelA-like and Pen-like functions may also be ancient like PelB, even though the primary sequence of these enhancers are no longer alignable because of turnover of binding sites at the DNA sequence level (Dermitzakis and Clark, 2002; Wray et al., 2003).
evidence: This is speculation about evolutionary mechanisms supported by citations.

claim: Genetic programs for producing morphologically distinct pectoral and pelvic appendages have existed since early periods of vertebrate evolution.
source: Genetic programs for producing morphologically distinct pectoral and pelvic appendages have clearly existed since early periods of vertebrate evolution, as shown by the distinct morphologies of pectoral and pelvic fins in stem gnathosomes, as well as the distinct forelimb and hind limb morphologies of stem tetrapods (Coates, 2003; Zhu et al., 2012; Shubin et al., 2014; Jeffery et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on fossil evidence.

claim: Hind limb and patellar abnormalities are relatively common in humans.
source: For example, hind limb and patellar abnormalities are relatively common in humans (Bongers et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2017; Basit and Khoshhal, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The PelB region can be examined for base pair changes, insertions, deletions, or copy number differences that may contribute to morphological traits or disease phenotypes in humans.

evidence: This is speculation about future applications of the findings.

claim: Benthic sticklebacks from Paxton Lake show almost complete loss of the pelvic apparatus.

evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Most of the variation in pelvic size in Paxton benthic fish has been linked to a 300 kb region surrounding the Pitx1 locus.

claim: PAXB fish have dual mutations in two different pelvic enhancers of the Pitx1 gene.

source: While the PelA enhancer is completely deleted (Chan et al., 2010)

claim: The PelB enhancer shows both a 125 bp deletion and a 341 bp insertion in PAXB fish.
source: the PelB enhancer shows both a 125 bp deletion and a 341 bp insertion in PAXB fish.
evidence: This is a primary finding from sequencing data.

claim: The inserted sequence in PAXB PelB is nearly identical to a region located approximately 3 kb upstream of the PelB region.
source: The inserted sequence is nearly identical to a region located approximately 3 kb upstream of the PelB region, suggesting the allele arose by concurrent duplication and local insertion of DNA.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and inference about the mechanism.

source: Paxton benthic fish do not show distinctive morphologies in their pectoral and median fins compared to other freshwater sticklebacks, though it is possible that subtle morphological changes have been missed.

claim: The dual mutations in both PelA and PelB in Paxton benthic fish likely contribute to the nearly complete loss of the pelvic apparatus in this population.

source: Stickleback PelB shows 51% identity to mouse PelB over a core 530 bp region.

source: We have now identified a novel enhancer from the mammalian Pitx1 gene that is located downstream rather than upstream of Pitx1 coding exons, in a region that is also known to interact directly with the Pitx1 promoter during hind limb development (Andrey et al., 2017; Kragesteen et al., 2018; Supplementary file 1B).
